cemc-fryer-2011-01a.title: Keep adding 3
cemc-fryer-2011-01a.body:
The 5th term is $14$. Adding the common difference $3$ gives the 6th term $14 + 3 = 17$, and adding $3$ again gives the 7th term $17 + 3 = 20$.

**Answer: 17 and 20**

cemc-fryer-2011-01b.title: Count the jumps
cemc-fryer-2011-01b.body:
To get from the 1st term to the 31st term we add $3$ thirty times. So the 31st term is $2 + 30 \times 3 = 92$.

**Answer: 92**

cemc-fryer-2011-01b.title: Compare with multiples of 3
cemc-fryer-2011-01b.body:
Each term is $1$ less than a multiple of $3$: the $n$th term is $3n - 1$ (check: $3(1) - 1 = 2$, $3(2)-1 = 5$). So the 31st term is $93 - 1 = 92$.

**Answer: 92**

cemc-fryer-2011-01c.title: Count the jumps
cemc-fryer-2011-01c.body:
From $2$ to $110$ is an increase of $108$. Since $108 \div 3 = 36$, we add $3$ thirty-six times, so there are $36 + 1 = 37$ terms (the first term plus one term per jump).

**Answer: 37**

cemc-fryer-2011-01c.title: Solve an equation
cemc-fryer-2011-01c.body:
The $n$th term is $3n - 1$. Solving $3n - 1 = 110$ gives $3n = 111$, so $n = 37$.

**Answer: 37**

cemc-fryer-2011-01d.title: Count jumps from the first term
cemc-fryer-2011-01d.body:
Every term equals $2$ plus some whole number of $3$s. For $1321$ to appear, $1321 - 2 = 1319$ would have to be a multiple of $3$. But $1319 = 3 \times 439 + 2$, so it is not.

Therefore $1321$ does **not** appear in the sequence.

cemc-fryer-2011-01d.title: Look at remainders
cemc-fryer-2011-01d.body:
Every term has remainder $2$ when divided by $3$ ($2, 5, 8, \dots$), since adding $3$ does not change the remainder. The digit sum of $1321$ is $7$, so $1321$ has remainder $1$ when divided by $3$ (because $1320$ is divisible by $3$).

So $1321$ is **not** a term of the sequence.

cemc-fryer-2011-02ai.title: Pythagorean Theorem
cemc-fryer-2011-02ai.body:
Since $AD$ bisects $BC$, $BD = 7$. Triangle $ADB$ has a right angle at $D$, so
$$AD^2 = AB^2 - BD^2 = 625 - 49 = 576,$$
and $AD = 24$.

**Answer: 24**

cemc-fryer-2011-02ai.title: Recognize a Pythagorean triple
cemc-fryer-2011-02ai.body:
Right triangle $ADB$ has hypotenuse $25$ and leg $BD = 7$. The triple $7, 24, 25$ is a well-known Pythagorean triple ($49 + 576 = 625$), so $AD = 24$.

**Answer: 24**

cemc-fryer-2011-02aii.title: Base times height
cemc-fryer-2011-02aii.body:
From part (i), the altitude is $AD = 24$. The area is $\frac12 \times BC \times AD = \frac12 \times 14 \times 24 = 168$.

**Answer: 168**

cemc-fryer-2011-02aii.title: Two right triangles
cemc-fryer-2011-02aii.body:
$\triangle ABC$ is made of two right triangles with legs $7$ and $24$. Each has area $\frac12 \times 7 \times 24 = 84$, so the total area is $168$.

**Answer: 168**

cemc-fryer-2011-02bi.title: Track the rotated sides
cemc-fryer-2011-02bi.body:
Rotation does not change lengths. When $\triangle ADB$ is rotated, side $AD$ becomes $PD$; when $\triangle ADC$ is rotated, side $AD$ becomes $RD$. So $PD = RD = AD = 24$.

Since $P$, $D$, $R$ lie on a line, $PR = 24 + 24 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

cemc-fryer-2011-02bi.title: Think of the new triangle's shape
cemc-fryer-2011-02bi.body:
In the new triangle the two altitudes $AD$ (each of length $24$) lie end to end along the base, while the half-bases $BD$ and $DC$ (each $7$) both point down to $Q$. So the base is $2 \times 24 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

cemc-fryer-2011-02bii.title: Base times height
cemc-fryer-2011-02bii.body:
After the rotation, side $DC$ becomes the altitude $DQ$, so $DQ = 7$. With base $PR = 48$, the area is $\frac12 \times 48 \times 7 = 168$.

**Answer: 168**

cemc-fryer-2011-02bii.title: Same pieces, same area
cemc-fryer-2011-02bii.body:
$\triangle PQR$ is made of exactly the same two pieces as $\triangle ABC$, just moved. Moving pieces does not change their area, so the area is still $168$ (from part (a)).

**Answer: 168**

cemc-fryer-2011-02c.title: Reverse the cut-and-rotate process
cemc-fryer-2011-02c.body:
Draw the altitude $YW$ to $XZ$. It bisects $XZ$, so $XW = WZ = 15$, and in right triangle $YWX$,
$$YW^2 = 17^2 - 15^2 = 289 - 225 = 64,$$
so $YW = 8$.

Now reverse the process of part (b): cut along $YW$ and rotate each half $90^\circ$ about $W$. The equal sides stay $17$, and the new base is made of two copies of $YW$, so it is $2 \times 8 = 16$. The area is unchanged: $\frac12 \times 16 \times 15 = 120$.

**Answer: the sides are 17, 17 and 16.**

cemc-fryer-2011-02c.title: Use the two right triangles directly
cemc-fryer-2011-02c.body:
An isosceles triangle with equal sides $17$ splits into two right triangles with hypotenuse $17$. For $\triangle XYZ$ the legs are $15$ and $8$ (since $15^2 + 8^2 = 17^2$), and the area is $15 \times 8 = 120$.

Swapping the roles of the legs (half-base $8$, height $15$) gives another isosceles triangle with sides $17, 17$ and base $16$, and area $\frac12 \times 16 \times 15 = 120$.

**Answer: 17, 17 and 16**

cemc-fryer-2011-03a.title: Just do it
cemc-fryer-2011-03a.body:
$68 \to 6 \times 8 = 48 \to 4 \times 8 = 32 \to 3 \times 2 = 6$.

The process stops at $6$ after $3$ steps.

**Answer: 3**

cemc-fryer-2011-03a.title: Reuse the example
cemc-fryer-2011-03a.body:
The first step gives $6 \times 8 = 48$. The example shows that $48$ needs $2$ more steps. So $68$ needs $1 + 2 = 3$ steps.

**Answer: 3**

cemc-fryer-2011-03b.title: Work backwards
cemc-fryer-2011-03b.body:
For the process to end at $8$, the number just before must have digit product $8$: these are $18, 81, 24, 42$ (from $1 \times 8$ and $2 \times 4$).

Now find the two-digit numbers whose digit product is each of these:

- $18 = 2 \times 9 = 3 \times 6$: $29, 92, 36, 63$
- $81 = 9 \times 9$: $99$
- $24 = 3 \times 8 = 4 \times 6$: $38, 83, 46, 64$
- $42 = 6 \times 7$: $67, 76$

(Factor pairs such as $1 \times 18$ do not work since $18$ is not a digit.)

**Answer: 29, 92, 36, 63, 99, 38, 83, 46, 64, 67, 76**

cemc-fryer-2011-03b.title: Check by forward computation
cemc-fryer-2011-03b.body:
Each listed number really takes two steps, e.g. $29 \to 18 \to 8$, $99 \to 81 \to 8$, $46 \to 24 \to 8$, $76 \to 42 \to 8$. Conversely, the second-to-last number must be a two-digit number with digit product $8$, i.e. one of $18, 81, 24, 42$, so working backwards (as in the first approach) finds every possibility and no others.

**Answer: 29, 92, 36, 63, 99, 38, 83, 46, 64, 67, 76**

cemc-fryer-2011-03c.title: Work backwards level by level
cemc-fryer-2011-03c.body:
**One step before 4:** two-digit numbers with digit product $4$: $14, 41, 22$.

**Before those:** digit product $14 = 2 \times 7$ gives $27, 72$; digit product $41$ is impossible ($41$ is prime and not a digit); digit product $22 = 2 \times 11$ is impossible.

**Before those:** digit product $27 = 3 \times 9$ gives $39, 93$; digit product $72 = 8 \times 9$ gives $89, 98$.

**Before those:** $39 = 3 \times 13$, $93 = 3 \times 31$, $89$ (prime) and $98 = 2 \times 49 = 7 \times 14$ cannot be written as a product of two digits, so we stop.

**Answer: 14, 41, 22, 27, 72, 39, 93, 89, 98**

cemc-fryer-2011-03c.title: Verify the chains
cemc-fryer-2011-03c.body:
The chains are
- $14 \to 4$, $41 \to 4$, $22 \to 4$
- $27 \to 14 \to 4$, $72 \to 14 \to 4$
- $39 \to 27 \to 14 \to 4$, $93 \to 27 \to 14 \to 4$
- $89 \to 72 \to 14 \to 4$, $98 \to 72 \to 14 \to 4$

Any number ending at $4$ must pass through a number with digit product $4$ just before the end, and the backward search covers every possibility at each level.

**Answer: 14, 41, 22, 27, 72, 39, 93, 89, 98**

cemc-fryer-2011-03d.title: Extend the chains from part (b) backwards
cemc-fryer-2011-03d.body:
In part (b), the numbers that stop at $8$ after 2 steps are $29, 92, 36, 63, 99, 38, 83, 46, 64, 67, 76$. To get more steps we need one of these to be a digit product:
- $63 = 7 \times 9$, from $79$ or $97$ — but neither $79$ nor $97$ is a digit product.
- $64 = 8 \times 8$, from $88$ — but $88$ is not a digit product.
- $36 = 4 \times 9$ (from $49$, $94$) or $6 \times 6$ (from $66$). And $49 = 7 \times 7$ comes from $77$!

So $77 \to 49 \to 36 \to 18 \to 8$ takes 4 steps.

**Answer: 77** (in fact it is the only one)

cemc-fryer-2011-04a.title: Start minus spent
cemc-fryer-2011-04a.body:
The jar starts with $365 \times \$2 = \$730$. Over 365 days Ian spends $365 \times \$1.72 = \$627.80$, and all change goes back into the jar. So the jar holds $\$730 - \$627.80 = \$102.20$.

**Answer: \$102.20**

cemc-fryer-2011-04a.title: Think per day
cemc-fryer-2011-04a.body:
Pair each day with one of the 365 two-dollar coins. Each day the tea costs $\$1.72 = \$2.00 - \$0.28$, so for each day $\$0.28$ of "its" coin's value stays in the jar. After 365 days the jar holds $365 \times \$0.28 = \$102.20$.

**Answer: \$102.20**

cemc-fryer-2011-04b.title: Bound, then show it happens
cemc-fryer-2011-04b.body:
Ian always has \$2 coins available (he uses at most one per day), so he never offers more than \$2.00. Hence his change is at most $200 - 172 = 28$¢, which contains at most one 25¢ coin. So the number of quarters rises by at most 1 per day.

**At most 7:** to reach 8 quarters, he would have needed 7 quarters the day before. But then he has at least $7 \times 25 = 175$¢ in loose change, so he pays with loose coins offering at most 175¢, getting at most 3¢ change — no quarter. So he can never reach 8.

**7 happens:** paying with a \$2 coin gives 28¢ change = one quarter and three pennies. After 6 days he has $6 \times 28 = 168$¢ $< 172$¢ in loose change, so on day 7 he again pays with a \$2 coin and then holds 7 quarters.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-fryer-2011-04b.title: Simulate the first week
cemc-fryer-2011-04b.body:
Day by day (loose change after paying):
- Days 1–6: each day pay \$2, receive 25¢ + 3 × 1¢. After day 6: 6 quarters, 18 pennies = 168¢.
- Day 7: 168¢ < 172¢, so pay \$2 again: 7 quarters, 21 pennies = 196¢.
- Day 8: now 196¢ ≥ 172¢ in loose coins. The closest amount ≥ 172¢ he can make is $7 \times 25 = 175$¢ (or with pennies, $6 \times 25 + 21 = 171$¢ is too small), so he hands over the quarters and the count drops to 0.

The pattern then repeats with at most 6 quarters per cycle (see the official table), and the argument in the first approach shows 8 is impossible. The maximum is 7.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-fryer-2011-04c.title: Find the cycle
cemc-fryer-2011-04c.body:
Call a day **typical** if Ian pays with a \$2 coin and receives one quarter and three pennies (28¢). Tracking the jar (loose change at the end of the day):

| Day | 7 | 8 | 14 | 15 | 21 | 22 | 28 | 29 | 35 | 36 | 42 | 43 | 49 | 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \$2 | 358 | 358 | 352 | 352 | 346 | 346 | 340 | 340 | 334 | 334 | 328 | 328 | 322 | 322 |
| 25¢ | 7 | 0 | 6 | 0 | 6 | 0 | 6 | 0 | 6 | 0 | 6 | 0 | 6 | 0 |
| 1¢ | 21 | 24 | 42 | 20 | 38 | 16 | 34 | 12 | 30 | 8 | 26 | 4 | 22 | 0 |

All omitted days are typical. On days 8, 15, 22, 29, 36, 43 and 50 Ian has enough loose change and pays with it.

After day 50 the jar contains only \$2 coins again ($365 - 322 = 43$ used), so the pattern repeats every 50 days. After 250 days there are $365 - 5 \times 43 = 150$ two-dollar coins and nothing else.

Day 277 is like day 27 of the cycle. Day 28 is typical with 340, 6, 34, so at the end of day 27 there are 341 two-dollar coins, 5 quarters and 31 pennies — i.e. $365 - 341 = 24$ two-dollar coins used in 27 days.

So after 277 days: $150 - 24 = 126$ two-dollar coins, 5 quarters and 31 pennies.

**Answer: 126 two-dollar coins, 5 quarters, 31 pennies**

cemc-fryer-2011-04c.title: Check with the total value
cemc-fryer-2011-04c.body:
After 277 days Ian has spent $277 \times \$1.72 = \$476.44$, so the jar must hold $\$730 - \$476.44 = \$253.56$. Indeed $126 \times \$2 + 5 \times \$0.25 + 31 \times \$0.01 = \$252 + \$1.25 + \$0.31 = \$253.56$. ✓

Why the cycle has length 50: the jar returns to only \$2 coins when the money spent, $172d$ cents, is a multiple of $200$. The least such $d$ is $\text{lcm}(172, 200)/172 = 8600/172 = 50$.
